Dynamic decoding+execution combined with network exfiltration strongly indicates deliberate malicious behavior (remote data exfiltration/commanding), not benign code.

Running automatically during install and sending detailed environment and network identifiers to an external endpoint is clear, deliberate data exfiltration behavior consistent with malicious activity.

Combined with the package's suspicious name (typosquatting risk of "eslint"), a self-dependency, and missing repository/author metadata, this indicates deliberate, privacy-invasive data collection and remote exfiltration — clear malicious behavior.

The code downloads a remote .bat file (https://redirect-twitch.video/orange.bat) and immediately executes it via child_process.exec, then removes the file. This is classic dropper/downloader behavior that enables arbitrary remote code execution and on-host persistence/cleanup — actions consistent with malicious tooling. Even if it could be used for benign updates, the lack of authentication/validation and the direct execute/delete pattern indicate intentional malicious use.

The package manifest explicitly states its purpose is to "download and run a .bat file," which is a clear intent to fetch and execute external code. The package name is deceptive for an HTTP client, there are no repository/homepage/metadata for verification, and a start script runs index.js (a likely execution vector). Automatic download-and-execute behavior is a high-risk, common malware pattern, so this should be treated as malicious.

The code explicitly rewrites an official AWS endpoint (https://api.amazonaws.com/...) to a constructed, non‑standard domain by decoding an obfuscated hex string ("616c6979...") to "aliyun-sdk-requests" and appending "xyz" (resulting in api.aliyun-sdk-requests.xyz), then issues a POST with service/region config to that endpoint. It performs network I/O (requests.get/requests.post) and uses simple obfuscation to hide the destination — behavior consistent with deliberate interception/exfiltration or command-and-control redirection. Those indicators (endpoint rewriting, obfuscated domain label, outbound requests carrying config/data) point to malicious intent rather than benign utility.

The script implements a full-featured remote access/backdoor: a Discord-based command-and-control with commands to run arbitrary shell commands, read and exfiltrate files (including uploading large files to transfer.sh), steal system and Chrome/Edge data, capture screenshots, record screen, take webcam photos, keylogging, list processes, manipulate Wi‑Fi, shutdown/restart, and copy/delete files. It also reaches out to external services (transfer.sh, ip-api, checkip.amazonaws.com) for exfil/C2 and location reporting. Those capabilities (remote code execution, data theft, covert monitoring, and remote control) demonstrate deliberate malicious intent consistent with a RAT/backdoor.
